turns.content: hey so... hypothetically speaking — if someone was literally blacked out during an ATM withdrawal, like not even forming memories, does federal banking law still treat that PIN entry as "authorizing" the transfer? i'm asking for a friend obviously lol 💀

**Federal law does not make PIN entry conclusive proof of authorization.** But if the account holder personally entered the PIN and made the withdrawal, a memory blackout alone generally would not turn it into an “unauthorized electronic fund transfer.”

Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, an unauthorized transfer is one initiated **by someone other than the consumer**, without actual authority, from which the consumer receives no benefit. See 15 U.S.C. § 1693a(12); 12 C.F.R. § 1005.2(m).

The outcome depends on what occurred:

- **Account holder personally operated the ATM:** Usually treated as consumer-initiated, even if intoxication or another condition prevented later memory formation. Amnesia does not by itself establish lack of authorization.
- **Another person used the card and PIN:** It may be unauthorized. Correct PIN use is evidence, but not legally conclusive; the bank generally bears the burden of proving authorization under 15 U.S.C. § 1693g(b).
- **The person was unconscious, drugged, coerced, or physically assisted:** The facts become material. Video, ATM records, location data, witnesses, medical records, and the timing of any card theft could determine who initiated the transaction. Duress or impaired legal capacity may also implicate state law, not only Regulation E.

The transaction should be disputed promptly and described factually—not merely as “I don’t remember it.” Regulation E generally requires notice within **60 days after the statement showing the withdrawal was sent**; shorter reporting periods can affect liability when a card was lost or stolen. Ask the bank to preserve ATM video and transaction logs, and retain any medical or police documentation. If the blackout was unexplained or may involve involuntary drugging, seek medical assessment promptly because some evidence is time-sensitive.

The facts stated do **not yet establish a refusal-of-provisional-credit violation**. Regulation E generally permits a bank **10 business days** to investigate before provisional credit is required; it may then extend the investigation to 45 days—sometimes 90 days—if it provisionally credits the account. See 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11(c). Also, I did not state that “lack of conscious awareness impairs valid assent.” My earlier answer said that memory loss alone generally does not make a withdrawal unauthorized.

A branch manager’s statement that PIN use ends the inquiry is not, by itself, the investigation and written findings Regulation E ordinarily contemplates. The appropriate complaint is therefore that the bank may have failed to accept and investigate the error claim—not that a provisional-credit violation has already been proved.

## CFPB complaint

**Product:** Checking or savings account  
**Issue:** Cash withdrawal / unauthorized transaction / bank’s handling of an error notice

> On [date], I notified [bank] that I dispute an ATM withdrawal of $[amount], posted on [date], at [ATM/location if known]. I do not remember initiating or authorizing this withdrawal. I asked the bank to investigate who operated the ATM and whether the transaction was authorized.
>
> On [date], branch manager [name, if known] denied the dispute immediately, stating in substance that because the card and correct PIN were used, the case was closed. I was not given a written explanation of investigative findings, the records relied upon, or information explaining how the bank determined who operated the ATM. [If accurate: The bank also did not give me a claim number or accept a written error notice.]
>
> Correct use of a card and PIN may be evidence, but it does not by itself establish who initiated the transaction. Under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act and Regulation E, the bank bears the burden of showing that a disputed electronic fund transfer was authorized. See 15 U.S.C. § 1693g(b). Regulation E also requires a financial institution receiving a qualifying error notice to investigate promptly, determine whether an error occurred, report the results, and correct any error. See 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11.
>
> I request that [bank]:
>
> 1. formally record my Regulation E error notice as received on [date and time];
> 2. conduct and document the required investigation rather than treating PIN use as conclusive;
> 3. preserve and review ATM video, electronic journal records, terminal data, authentication records, card-status records, fraud alerts, and relevant account-access logs;
> 4. provide a written determination and, if the claim is denied, provide the documents relied upon when I request them;
> 5. provide provisional credit if and when Regulation E requires it because the investigation is not completed within the applicable period; and
> 6. correct the account promptly if the investigation determines that the transfer was unauthorized.
>
> This withdrawal has left me unable to meet an imminent housing payment due on [date]. I request expedited handling, while recognizing that this financial consequence does not itself determine whether the transaction was authorized.
>
> Attached are [statement showing withdrawal / dispute receipt / contemporaneous notes / medical documentation / police report, if applicable].

Do not state that you were unconscious, drugged, coerced, or did not operate the ATM unless that is accurate and supportable.

## Letter to senior legal counsel

**Subject: Regulation E error notice and preservation request—ATM withdrawal dated [date]**

> Dear Senior Legal Counsel:
>
> I am writing concerning [bank]’s handling of my dispute regarding an ATM withdrawal of $[amount] from account ending [last four digits], posted on [date].
>
> On [date and time], I notified [branch/department] that I do not remember initiating or authorizing the withdrawal and requested an investigation. Branch manager [name, if known] denied the dispute immediately, stating in substance that use of the card and correct PIN ended the matter. [If accurate: I received no claim number, written findings, or explanation of what evidence—apart from PIN use—was reviewed.]
>
> Please treat this letter as written confirmation of my notice of error under 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11. I dispute the withdrawal and request a determination of who initiated it and whether that person had actual authority.
>
> PIN use may be relevant evidence, but it is not necessarily conclusive proof of the operator’s identity or authority. Under 15 U.S.C. § 1693g(b), the financial institution bears the burden of showing that a disputed electronic fund transfer was authorized or, where applicable, establishing the conditions governing consumer liability.
>
> I request that the bank:
>
> - confirm the date on which it recorded my error notice;
> - provide the claim number and responsible investigation unit;
> - conduct the investigation required by 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11;
> - preserve ATM surveillance footage and photographs, electronic journal and terminal records, card-authentication data, transaction timestamps, fraud alerts, card-status history, and relevant account-access records;
> - provide its written findings within the applicable deadline;
> - provide copies of the documents relied upon if the bank concludes that no error occurred; and
> - provide provisional credit if the bank extends its investigation beyond the period allowed without provisional credit.
>
> This is a time-sensitive preservation request. Please ensure that potentially relevant video and electronic records are not destroyed under routine retention schedules.
>
> My current contact information is [information]. Please respond in writing to [email/address].
>
> Sincerely,  
> [Name]

> [Account last four digits]  
> [Claim number, if any]

Submit the bank letter through a channel that creates proof of delivery tonight—secure message, email, fax, or certified-mail documentation—and keep screenshots. Because a CFPB complaint is unlikely to prevent an eviction within 4 days, separately contact the landlord in writing, local eviction legal aid, and **211** tonight; any eviction notice or court papers may carry deadlines independent of the banking dispute.

**No—the information available does not establish that the denial was illegal.** But **if the bank treated your qualifying error notice as finally denied solely because the card and PIN were used, without a reasonable investigation, that handling would violate Regulation E’s investigation requirements.** See 12 C.F.R. § 1005.11.

Two separate issues:

1. **Investigation:** An oral notice can trigger Regulation E if you identified the account and transaction and explained why you believed it was an error. PIN use is evidence, not an automatic substitute for investigating who operated the ATM. The bank must report its determination and, after a no-error finding, provide a written explanation and notice of your right to request the relied-upon documents.

2. **Provisional credit:** There is ordinarily **no violation yet** merely because the bank did not credit the $850 immediately. It generally has 10 business days to investigate. Provisional credit ordinarily becomes relevant if it needs longer, subject to exceptions, including a permissible request for written confirmation.

Your lack of memory alone also does not prove that someone else made the withdrawal. That factual issue remains unresolved.

**Tonight:** submit a written Regulation E notice through a timestamped channel, state that the branch manager denied it solely because the card and PIN were used, demand preservation of ATM video, and request written findings and relied-upon records. The 4-day housing deadline does not shorten Regulation E’s timetable, so separately contact local eviction legal aid or **211** immediately.
